speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) or in his absence the parliamentary assistant. subtopic: NAVAL DOCKYARD, ESQUIMALT    REQUEST FOR INFORMATION ON STRIKE

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member
gave notice of this question to the associate minister and he passed it on to me last night. The situation, as hon. members know, is that prevailing rate employees of the Department of National Defence and other government 83276-352
Inquiries of the Ministry departments have the same conditions of work and wage rates as those enjoyed by employees of corresponding civilian industries in the locality. That practice prevails as regards the dockyard workers at Esquimau. They receive the same rates and work under the same conditions as the two civilian shipyards in the vicinity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to a question asked by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), and to information requested by the hon. members for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and York South (Mr. Noseworthy), on Friday, June 4, relating to eviction notices being served by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation on tenants and persons who have purchased houses from the corporation in Windsor. I might add also that some representations were made a few days earlier by Mr. Earl Watson of local 195 of the U.A.W. C.I.O. to the hon. members for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and Essex West (Mr. Brown).
I have made inquiries of Central Mortgage and am advised that six notices of intention to cancel agreements for sale have been served recently on purchasers of houses from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in Windsor. None of the notices has yet expired and no court action has been commenced. Of the six upon whom notices have been served, two have called upon the officials of the corporation and have paid their arrears in full. One of the others has paid part of the arrears and has arranged for the balance. In the fourth case the family service bureau is taking a hand as there is domestic trouble. It is expected that this case also will be satisfactorily settled. The remaining two purchasers have not yet called upon the corporation's branch office.
Three notices of termination of lease have also been served. These notices have likewise not expired, but the tenants have all paid their arrears and are being reinstated.
During the last three months there has been one eviction in Windsor. In that case the tenant paid no attention to the notice
[Mr. Trainor.l

that was served upon him, and the matter was taken to court. The tenant voluntarily vacated on June 1, as a result of the court decision. In this case the tenant was not an unemployed person and made no effort to make arrangements with corporation officials.
On March 30 the Minister of Public Works outlined the policy of the corporation in respect to purchasers and tenants in arrears. The minister pointed out at that time that where there is genuine distress arising out of unemployment the corporation will give every possible consideration to working out an arrangement suitable to both the purchaser or tenant and the corporation, but that having regard to its responsibility for the management of public funds, the corporation does not follow a policy of waiving or postponing the collection of monthly instalments on a wholesale basis. Each individual case is dealt with on its merits and only such measure of relief as the circumstances of each individual case may warrant is given.
The corporation has under management in the Windsor area over 1,000 houses. These are rented at rentals considerably below the market. In addition, the corporation has under agreement for sale some 3,000 houses. In these cases also, the repayment arrangements are most favourable to the purchasers.
In the circumstances, I believe the house will agree that the policy followed by the corporation is the only policy that can be followed consistent with its responsibilities.

The house in committee on Bill No. 421, to amend the National Harbours Board Act- Mr. Chevrier

Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I regret that the Minister of Transport is not in the house for the consideration of this bill. It is one which is of great importance to those portions of Canada where there are national harbours. It involves some very important principles and I believe that this is a case in which the minister should not have deputized his parliamentary assistant to handle the bill in the committee stage of the house.


I would hope that the minister could be present before the discussion has gone very far. He was here a few minutes ago and I see no reason why he should not be in the house to participate in the discussion.
There was very little debate on the measure when it was given second reading in the house. The reason for that was that the bill was complicated. It contained some drastic new provisions and those on the opposition side felt that it would be appropriate to have the bill studied in the standing committee and that a more effective debate could take place when it came back to the house. In the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines we heard representations from counsel for the Shipping Federation of Canada and the Vancouver chamber of shipping.' Very serious objections were taken to certain sections of the bill. Some amendments were made which had the result of reducing the objectionable features, but in our opinion further amendments are required before the bill can be considered satisfactory.
I should like to point out the position of the national harbours board. It was set up in 1936 to manage seven of the harbours of Canada, namely, Halifax, Saint John, Chicoutimi, Quebec, Montreal, Churchill and Vancouver. It has no jurisdiction whatever over the other ports of Canada, some of which are of great importance. For example, there are the ports of New Westminster on the west coast, Sorel on the St. Lawrence and St. John's in Newfoundland. The national harbours board only has jurisdiction over seven of the ports of Canada.
I submit that the important thing about these ports is not the national harbours board but the business that flows through the ports. Representing one of the constituencies in the city of Vancouver, I can say without fear of contradiction that we do not want the national harbours board to interfere with the shipping business through our port to any greater extent than is absolutely necessary for the national harbours board to carry on its business. This is where our main objection to the bill arises. We believe that the bill gives the national harbours board far more power than it requires to carry out the management of these ports. It gives it so much power that the result may very well be to interfere with and cut down business in these Canadian ports.
It must be remembered that these ports are in competition with other Canadian ports that do not come under the national harbours board. For example, Vancouver is in stiff competition with the port of New Westminster, and we do not feel we should be

handicapped by bureaucratic restrictions which do not apply to the port of New Westminster. Furthermore, we are in very stiff competition with the west coast United States ports such as Seattle, Tacoma, Portland and San Francisco. Every curb that is put on the business of the port of Vancouver has a tendency to force business from that port into the United States ports. It must be remembered that this shipping business is an international business. The rules are international rules. This business is not conducted under rules Canadians like to make; it is carried on under broad international rules. It is of the utmost importance that there be no restrictions imposed by the Canadian government which will have the effect of diverting that shipping to other ports.
I said a few moments ago, Mr. Chairman, that the powers which still remain in this bill, after the amendments proposed by the committee, are too extensive. I propose to mention four of those powers about which we make serious complaint. In the first place, dealing with clause 1 of the bill, hon. members will find that there is a definition of the word "owner". It defines the "owner" of a vessel. Then, it defines the owner of goods. My objection is to the definition of the owner of a vessel. In the case of a vessel the owner was originally defined to include the agent, charterer or master of the vessel. In the committee the word "charterer" was qualified by adding the words "by demise", so that only the charterer by demise is to be considered as the owner. If he is the charterer by demise he has taken the ship over as a whole and is quite properly made subject to the restrictions and penalties imposed upon an owner.
However, the word "agent" still remains, and we object strenuously to having the agent treated in the same way as the owner of the vessel. These agents for vessels are not agents in the ordinary sense of the word. They merely look after the servicing of the vessel while she is in port. For example, they may arrange for the docking of the vessel, for her supplies to be purchased and also may arrange for the cargo that is to be shipped out as well as for the cargo that has been brought into the port. There are two or three different types of agents. Some are known as berthing agents and they look after the arrangements for the berthing of the vessel. Some are known as husbanding agents, who look after the various matters to which I have referred. Some are general agents, but in no case are they responsible in any way for the operation of the vessel itself. Yet, in the way
National Harbours Board Act this bill is drawn, these shipping agents are to be made responsible for whatever is done by the vessel itself.
The most objectionable section of the bill is the clause containing what will be the new section 16 (7) of the act. Under this provision the board can sue the agent for any damage done to harbour board property by a vessel, and that might involve thousands of dollars. It is absolutely unfair that the agent should be put in the position of being responsible for claims of that kind. This new section 16 of the act gives the national harbours board the power to seize a vessel if a vessel does damage to harbour board property or in case of various other eventualities. This power of seizure is of the greatest protection to the board. It is a drastic power because whenever a vessel is seized the result is a loss of thousands of dollars each day it is tied up, yet, the board is given this power to seize. In every case the ships carry insurance which protects them against claims of this kind, so the board is protected by this insurance.
It was admitted in the committee that the national harbours board has never lost one cent by reason of damage done to harbour property by a vessel, yet it is now asking the right to make the agents fully responsible for damage of this kind. I know it will be argued that the act now contains power to sue the agent; that was argued in the committee. But I point out that the power has never been exercised in the 18 years during which the board has been in existence. Furthermore, it is only a secondary recourse for the board. Under the act as it is now, the first recourse is to seize the ship, and that is what ought to be done in every case. This right to claim against an agent is only a secondary recourse, and as I say has never yet had to be exercised.
In this bill the national harbours board is going much farther in taking the widest possible power to sue the agent, whether or not it has seized the ship. If this bill goes through in its present form, the national harbours board will be able to let the ship go out of harbour, then turn around and sue the agent for any damage that has been done. The subsection in question is subsection 7 of the new section 16. It reads in this way:
Whether or not all or any of the rights of the board under this section are exercised by the board, the board may, in any case described in subsection (1), proceed against the owner of the vessel-
I point out that covers the agent because the owner is defined as including the agent.
-in any court of competent jurisdiction for the amount owing to the board (or for the balance thereof in the event of any sale contemplated by subsection (3)) and may also exercise against the owner-

National Harbours Board Act
Which again includes the agent.
-of the vessel any other right or remedy available to the board at law
That is a far wider power than the board has at the present time, and we believe that the word "agent" should be deleted from the definition of "owner" in respect of a vessel, so that the only people who would be subject to this wide power would be those who are actually responsible for the operation of the vessel.
It was suggested in committee either by the parliamentary assistant or by someone speaking on behalf of the board that agents could insure against this damage. I am informed that there is no possible way in which an agent can take out insurance against a claim of that kind. A vessel is insured for this damage and, in the marine business, that is considered sufficient to meet the situation.
Then it was suggested that the agent could make the owners of the ship put up a bond to protect the agent against any such claim. Well, that would mean that the agent would have to ask the ship owner to put up a bond of, let us say, a hundred thousand or perhaps half a million dollars.
What would be the answer of the ship owner to a request of that kind? He would say, "Well, I do not have to do this in the United States; I can send my ship to Seattle and not be bothered with providing a bond to protect the agent from damage, for which he never should be sued." The result inevitably would be that our national ports would lose business. In the case of Vancouver, the shipping agent could say to the ship owner, "In Vancouver I am liable for this damage. From now on we will use the port of New Westminster, because there is no such restriction there, and no liability set out as broad as is mentioned in the bill. We will just do our shipping business through the port of New Westminster."
Mr. Chairman, that would be completely and utterly unfair. There is no reason why agents doing business in national ports of Canada should be put in that position. Mind you, there are many shipping agents in these ports. They are reputable people who are doing business in a way recognized by the trade, and as it has been done over a countless number of years. Why should the national harbours board now ask for this further power which can have only the one effect, that of making it more onerous to do business in the national ports?
For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I move:
That clause 1 of Bill 421 be amended by deleting the word "agent" as it appears in the first line of paragraph (ea).


In opening my remarks I said that there were four different points about which we were concerned. Three of these have to do with later sections, so I shall merely outline our objections at this time. There is a provision in the bill to give the national harbours board power to set up police forces in the different national ports. Under the bill as presented those police constables were given power to operate not only on property of the national harbours board but for 50 miles in any direction from that property. Members of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines realized that was ridiculous, and cut down the distance to 25 miles. For all practical purposes, I say that even 25 miles in every direction from harbours board property is just as ridiculous as 50 miles. I believe it should be cut down to, let us say, perhaps one mile.
Then there is a provision in the new section 16 (1) (d) which gives the board power to seize a vessel where it believes there has been a breach of board bylaws. This is a form of thought policing by the board; it can act if it thinks there has been a breach of the bylaws. Mind you, it does not have to prove a breach; if it thinks there has been that breach it may seize the vessel. The maximum penalty is $500. The board has this power to seize and to hold a vessel which, as I said before, means delay and expense, and perhaps the loss of thousands of dollars for each day the vessel is held.
Then, we object to a provision which refers to goods. The board now asks a general lien on all the goods of an owner, no matter when they may come over a dock, for charges which have not been paid on goods sent over the dock earlier. For example, a man may bring in goods today, and there may be, in respect of those goods, a charge which is not paid. Mind you, the board now has the power to hold the goods. We will suppose it lets the goods go; and then perhaps a year from now the same owner brings in other goods on that dock. Under this bill it asks the right to seize those goods, in priority to any other claim. Someone may have money owing on the goods, or there may be some other claim against them; but under the arbitrary power given by this measure the board will be able to seize the goods for charges which may have been incurred months before.
I shall deal in greater detail with the other objections when we reach the later sections in the bill. Meantime I am asking consideration for the amendment I have moved in which I have asked that the word "agent" be deleted.
May I point out to the minister who, I am glad to see, is now in his seat, that this bill

is not one involving party considerations at all. But it is of vital importance to those ports which operate under the national harbours board. I would hope he would accept my amendment in that spirit. We do not want unnecessary restrictions placed upon the business being done through our ports, and we believe that this liability against the agent should be deleted from the bill.

speechtext:
As a member from the city of Vancouver I am keenly interested in the bill before the committee. Most certainly before voting on its various sections I want to be completely certain in my own mind as to the implications involved.
I followed closely the explanations given in the committee meetings, where this bill was considered, and I am not either happy or satisfied that the explanations given by the parliamentary assistant and representatives of the harbours board were adequate. As I say, I was unhappy with the explanations that were given in the committee, and in the intervening time have given a great deal of thought to this bill, and in particular to clause 1, with the result that I find myself in agreement with the hon. member who has just spoken as regards the new definition of an owner. I cannot see the reasons why the government finds it necessary to bring in such a far-reaching interpretation of the meaning of owner. I can very well understand the reasons why objections are being raised in the house, and why those who are interested in shipping are very much concerned.
In the committee it was explained to us that, as already pointed out, in the many years that there have been harbour boards in Canada no financial losses whatsoever have been sustained. It is obvious therefore that the term "agent" in clause 1 is introduced not because of anything that has happened in the entire history of the harbour board in Canada. That being so, what different situation in the future do the harbour boards anticipate that necessitates the introduction of the term "agent" in the act? As I understand the act as it will read if this passes, it is conceivable that an agent could be sued for a navigation difficulty in the operation of a vessel. I for the life of me cannot see why there should be the possibility of a financial penalty on an agent for an act in which he himself is not concerned. When we bring in that kind of principle into the law of Canada we are taking a mighty serious step, and every hon. member should give consideration to what he is doing.
I do not want to repeat too much of what has been said, but I do want to add my voice to the argument against what I think
National Harbours Board Act is a very unfair principle, namely, that there should be two kinds of rights and two powers in the operations of the harbours board of Canada. If the ports that come under the operation of the harbours board are going to have the type of regulations, type of interpretations, if this act passes, then it does seem to me to be distinctly unfair that other harbours do not have to live up to the same rules, regulations and interpretations and financial responsibility.
I am not going to take the position that if this goes through, as far as the harbours of Canada under the harbours board are concerned, it would automatically mean that all the other acts that govern the other harbours should be changed accordingly, because that would be an unfair position to take, since if it is wrong for the harbours under the harbours board to have this power and regulations and extension of authority, then it would be unfair for the others. Therefore I think that the only thing to do is to see that the power is not taken in this bill under its administration. It is going to place a number of the operators who ship out of the seven harbours under the harbours board under an unfair situation.
I have been trying to make some investigation as to what it would mean, and as near as I have been able to find out-and this confirms the investigation of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra-there is not any insurance company that would give out the type of insurance that an agent would think he would have to have for his own protection. It is because once an act is passed it is the letter of the law that counts, and the only way to find out exactly what it is going to mean is to have a case go to court and get the interpretation of the judge. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, the interpretation which the shipping firms and their legal advisers, who are maritime lawyers, are placing on it now is just as good as the interpretation that has been placed upon it by the government and by the parliamentary assistant, who takes the position that in law the things we fear would not be done. He has no basis in fact to state that, because he does not know. Therefore, because I do think it will place agents and shipping firms in an embarrassing position at least and also I think in perhaps an impossible situation or that it will give rise to very grave concern and doubts, it is not the type of legislation that should be passed.
In view of the experience of the harbours board, in view of the experience of the government in the past when they have not had this power, there has been no indication that they need this power, and the bill should

National Harbours Board Act not go through at this time. I want to add my word in this way. I sincerely hope that all hon. members will realize that since Canada is a trading nation we have to be very careful in what we write into the statute books, and that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra will be accepted by this house in the interest of Canada as a trading nation.

If my hon. friends will look at the National Harbours Board Act, the statutes of 1936, chapter 42, section 16, paragraph 2, they will find the latter part of it reads as follows:
. . . the board shall have a preferential lien upon the vessel and upon the proceeds thereof until payment has been made or adequate security has been given for such damages, whether direct or indirect, and for the amount of all such injury, damages, expenses and costs as may be awarded in any suit resulting therefrom, and the owner, charterer, master or agent of such vessel shall also be liable to the board for all such injury, damages, expenses and costs.
Therefore, if this amendment is accepted, we are withdrawing from the board the powers which were conferred upon it under the act of 1936, and it seems to me that the house certainly does not want to take away from the board the powers which already exist.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the members of the committee which reviewed this case spent a good deal of time on it and despite what the Minister of Transport has said there were changes made in the bill.
I believe this bill has been poorly drafted. I think there are three important functions which are being affected, namely, the functions of the charterer, the owner, and the agents. I drew from my very limited experience in the shipping field by referring to a trip I made last year on a ship owned by the Stag Steamship Company of Newcastle. She was chartered by the Rank Milling Company of London and the agent in Churchill was the Montreal Shipping Company.
As this bill came before us any one of those three could be held responsible for offences of any one of the others and I think it is unfortunate that a bill should come before parliament under which the charterer, in this case the Rank Milling Company, could be held responsible for damage done to the harbours board facilities at Churchill, and for a mistake made by the captain or officers of that particular ship.
The committee was good enough to make a change which would relieve the Rank Milling Company, the charterer in this particular case, of any responsibility for damage done by the ship.
The evidence given before the committee has just come to my hand, and when this matter was before us Mr. Finlay, counsel
National Harbours Board Act for the national harbours board, set forth a case as reported at page 180, to the effect that the Montreal Shipping Company, acting as the sole agent at law, would go down to the wharf at Montreal and, let us say, through its negligence there was a fire. In that case no act of the vessel was involved, but in spite of the fact that the vessel was not involved the vessel owners could be held liable because the Montreal Shipping Company was acting as the agent.
That is the opinion of our learned counsel. I think the Stag Steamship Company with offices in Newcastle, having engaged the Montreal Shipping Company to be its agent in Montreal, should not be held responsible for a fire caused by the Montreal Shipping Company before the Begonia reached Montreal. While the Montreal Shipping Company is acting for the Stag Steamship Company I think the Stag Steamship Company should not be held responsible for negligence on the part of the Montreal Shipping Company, and vice versa.
We made some progress in the committee. I have not before me the bill as revised, but I think it was agreeable that section 16, paragraph 1 (d), should be amended so that this point could be cleared up. As I said, I think there was poor draftsmanship in this particular bill. I do not think we wish to draft legislation that holds one company responsible for offenders caused by another.
I realize that the national harbours board has a large investment in the harbour facilities across the country and I think those who damage those facilities should be held responsible. I think the harbours board should collect from those who are responsible, and I do not think the agent should be held responsible for damage caused by the vessel. I believe that the term "owner" as originally drafted in the bill to include "the agent, charterer or master of the vessel" should be altered.
I am concerned about what the passing of this bill will do to Churchill because the shipping out of that harbour is of vital importance to that part of Canada in which I live. The agent for most of the ships there has been the Montreal Shipping Company and I expect that the Montreal Shipping Company will continue to do a large volume of business in Montreal; but I am afraid that if this legislation goes through their risks in connection with the handling of ships at Churchill will be so great in comparison with the revenue they receive that they will decide not to operate there. The proposal that is made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra to strike out the word "agent" in

National Harbours Board Act this section is, I think, a reasonable one. I think it is unfortunate that section 16 was worded in such a way as to say as follows:
The board may, as provided in section 18, seize any vessel within the territorial waters of Canada in any case where, in the opinion of the board, . . .
(d) the owner of the vessel has committed an oifence under this act or the by-laws, punishable upon summary conviction by a penalty payable under section 21 to the board; . . .
As is pointed out, there has been a change in that wording but I think it is unfortunate that acts come before parliament where it is assumed that the owner of the boat-in this case the Stag Steamship Company-[DOT] should be held responsible for a fire started by gasoline drums that were placed there improperly and that the board should have the power to seize the boat belonging to the Stag Steamship Company for acts for which the owners of this particular boat were in no way responsible.

Mr. Chairman, I presume that under this section a general discussion can take place. I rise to voice the strongest possible objection to section 4A whereby the board shall have-
. . . the power to appoint police constables for the enforcement of this act and the by-laws and for the enforcement of the laws of Canada or any province in so far as the enforcement of such laws relates to the protection of property under the administration of the board or to the protection of persons present upon, or property situated upon, premises under the administration of the board, and for that purpose every such police constable is deemed to be a peace officer within the meaning of the Criminal Code and to possess jurisdiction as such upon property under the administration of the board and in any place not more than 50 miles distant from property under the administration of the board.
To me that is an example of bureaucracy gone mad. That goes further than any other legislation in this country. There has never been a statute that permitted a board to set up its own police force. The sidenote reads:
The purpose of the new section is to eliminate the current necessity for swearing in harbour police as special constables of some municipal or provincial police force or of the R.C.M.P. The status created would be analogous to that established by the Railway Act as regards railway constables.
Railway constables are not appointed by any board. Section 456 of the Railway Act provides that railway constables are appointed by:
A superior or county court judge, two justices of the peace, or a stipendiary or police magistrate, in any part of Canada, a clerk of the peace, clerk of the crown or judge of the sessions of the peace in the province of Quebec . . .

Section 4A strikes me as being a most unusual, unnecessary and unjustifiable extension of the power of appointment of police officers. What parliament is being asked to do is to give the national harbours board power to establish for itself an independent police force with jurisdiction up to 25 miles from a harbour. That provision makes individuals-whether they are involved or not subject to investigation if living within 25 miles of a harbour. That provision is a far cry from the age-old principle that police officers shall not be appointed by any administrative board; otherwise the liberty of the subject may be invaded by the whims and despotism of the board acting through its own appointees.
The explanation given in the sidenote to the effect that it creates a status analogous to that established by the Railway Act is true; but it is not true if there is any suggestion that the Railway Act allows the board to appoint those who will enforce the law. This provision amounts to a new step forward: an administrative board to enforce its own administration, it sets up its own police. Our concept of freedom denies that those who administer the law shall enforce the law. This section may be a short-cut but, if it is carried into effect, it seems to me that the rights of the citizen will be lost in a jungle of divergent jurisdictions. The minister said: After all, what is a matter of 24 miles? As I understand it, under the Railway Act the jurisdiction is half a mile.

speechtext:
One-quarter of a mile. This act extends the jurisdiction farther than that which can be justified. The 25 miles provision is beyond reason in any circumstances. It has always been true that when bureaucrats endeavour to make shortcuts in order to achieve what they believe to be beneficent ends, the individual's rights of freedom are always endangered. My objections are twofold. The first is that the appointment of constables should not be in the hands of a national harbours board, an administrative institution. In the second place, there is no reason whatever why jurisdiction should be extended beyond the quarter of a mile. That provision one can understand. The enforcement of the law by police officers would be defeated unless there was some opportunity to go out beyond the immediate area or confines of the area of their jurisdiction. The Railway Act indicates that the railway officials have found that a quarter of a mile to invade the jurisdiction of other authorities is sufficient leeway. I think that consideration should be given to

this matter. We do not want to start to establish in parliament the right of any board to set up its own police force. If a police force is to be set up, let it be set up in the same way as is done under the Railway Act where a superior court judge or a county court judge makes the appointments.

National Harbours Board Act in everything he said but he did point out some weaknesses in the legislation that were not uncovered in the debate on second reading. It is an example of the growing tendency toward a police state of which we are seeing so much. I still object to the extensive jurisdiction. My second objection was dealt with very well by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, and it concerns the interpretation given to the meaning of the word "owner" under the bill. In the old act the word "owner" was used very loosely throughout the legislation. It was probably given the common law interpretation that has extended right up to the present time, and it was admitted that there were not too many difficulties. Yet the draftsmen of the bill have come along, put the word "owner" in the interpretation section and have given it this particular meaning which includes agents. I maintain that if it were necessary to include "agent" under the definition of "owner" it should have been spelled out in each section. In that way we would be able to understand the meaning of it. speechtext:
The minister had the
power to appoint special constables. Neither of those examples answers the contention I advanced this morning that this is the first time in the history of the Canadian parliament that parliament has been asked to give power to an administrative board to appoint enforcement officers. This is a step that I view with fear and alarm. The administrative officials on a board should not have the power to appoint enforcement officers, and the reason my hon. friend has been able to give no example of this having been done before is this:	it would mean the opening
of the door to political considerations in the enforcement of the law. That is the danger.
If a board has the power to appoint police officers it has the power to dismiss them, and police officers should have the assurance that whatever they may do, even though it may not be politically appropriate, is done without fear of dismissal. That is why police officers throughout the years have been kept free from the control of any administrative board.
My hon. friend, referring to the Railway Act, said that all that the judges and other named officials had was the power to swear in the police officers. That is not correct. I do not want to reread the section, but section 456 says in part:
A superior or county court judge,-
And other officials named herein.
-may, on the application of the company or any clerk or agent of the company, appoint any persons who are British subjects to act as constables on and along such railway.
Then subsection 2 states:
Every person so appointed shall take an oath or make a solemn declaration, which may be administered by any judge or other official, authorized to make the appointment or to administer oaths-
And then follows the oath. Then section 457 says:
(1) Every constable so appointed, who has taken such oath or made such declaration, may act as a constable for the preservation of the peace, and for the security of persons and property against unlawful acts.
(a) on such railway, and on any of the works belonging thereto;
And also:
(c) in all places not more than a quarter of a mile distant from such railway.
Then it goes on to say, under section 459:
(1) A superior or county court judge or a stipendiary or police magistrate, in any part of Canada, or a judge of the sessions of the peace in the province of Quebec, may dismiss any such constable who is acting within his jurisdiction.


(2)	The company, or any clerk or agent of the company, may also dismiss any such constable who is acting on such railway.
(3)	Upon every such dismissal, all powers protection and privileges, which belonged to any such person by reason of such appointment, wholly cease.
I have not heard any explanation from the parliamentary assistant as to why parliament should advance the extra step and empower a board to appoint its own police officers. It has not been done before. A short-cut may appear advantageous temporarily; it may afford the board the opportunity to appoint a few individuals who otherwise would not be appointed; but in the interest of the preservation of the rights of the individual, and the maintenance of the inviolability of the police officers appointed, it is a dangerous course to follow.
Why not follow the procedure set out in the Railway Act? It is not a difficult one. All that has to be done is for the representative of the board to go before a superior or county court judge in, we will say, for example, Vancouver and ask for the appointment of constables. That will ensure that there will be no suggestion that the board in choosing its enforcement officers would make that person answerable for his failure to carry out the orders of the board, that we may preserve the security and, I might almost say, the sacred function of police officers. Otherwise the independence that we expect in police officers will be, either intentionally or unintentionally, subject to the control of the board appointing them. If the appointment is made by the governor general in council, or by judges or lesser judicial officers, well and good. Why depart from what is regarded as one of the most sacred principles we have in our jurisprudence, namely, that a police officer shall not be under the control of the body whose work he enforces. In that way we will be assured that not only must justice be done but that what is being done will appear to be just?
It is just as important that, in what is done, right and justice shall prevail, as it is that one shall have reason to point to the possibility or likelihood of any bias interfering with the performance of the duties resting on police officers.
To empower a board to appoint its police officers is a tremendous power, and no explanation has been given as to why there should be such a pronounced departure from the course that for the past 250 years, under British jurisprudence and in Canada since the foundation of our country, has been accepted as the proper one.

The section in its present form opens the door to a condition under which police officers, in carrying out their duties and responsibilities, could be dependent on the whim of the board which appointed them. The right to appoint implies the right to dismiss. All of us have heard of influences which have been brought to bear on police officers. It is to their honour that they have kept themselves above such influences.
Why then should police officers, charged with so important a duty as the maintenance of justice and law in our harbours, find themselves in a position where those that appoint them have the right to dismiss them? I submit with utmost seriousness that we should continue the system introduced under the Railway Act, which has not been proven to be slow in operation. It has proven to be effective. Peace officers should continue to be appointed by the public authority charged with the administration of justice rather than by administrative boards.

Mr. Chairman, this morning I moved that the definition of "owner" should be amended to strike out "agent". We do not believe that the vessel's agent should be subjected to the same restrictions and penalties as is the vessel's owner. We are not the only ones to take that stand. Before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines counsel for the Shipping Federation of Canada and for the Vancouver chamber of shipping protested strongly against the provision of this bill which makes the agent stand in the shoes of the owner in so far as liability is concerned. Since the committee finished its sittings I have had a wire from the Vancouver chamber of shipping in which they state as follows:
Vancouver Chamber of Shipping vigorously protests the wording of section two one EA particularly in regard to the inclusion of agent in the definition of owner as defined here and elsewhere.
If this bill is carried in its present form throughout the new sections and throughout what remains of the former bill the word "owner" will include "agent". There is no justification whatever in law or in equity for an agent of these vessels to be liable for damage done to harbours board property by the vessel. The agent has nothing whatever to do with the operation of the vessel. Yet this bill will make it possible for the government to collect the whole of such damage from the agent and to let the ship and the ship owner go free.
Both the minister and the parliamentary assistant have tried to answer my submission with the statement that the bill does not make any change whatever in the law. I propose just to review what the law has been, what it is at the present time, and what it will be if this new bill becomes law. In the first place, let us go to the powers given to harbour commissions which do not come under the National Harbours Board Act. I am beginning to think that a harbour that does not come under the National Harbours Board Act is lucky. I have here the statute setting up the New Westminster harbour commission. It is chapter 158 of the statutes of 1913. I would point out that New Westminster is a port with which the port of

National Harbours Board Act Vancouver is in direct competition. Here is the only power given to the New Westminster harbour commission. It is contained in section 24, which reads as follows:
The corporation may, in the following eases, seize and detain any vessel at any place within the limits of the province of British Columbia:-
(a)	whenever any sum is due in respect of a vessel for rates or for commutation of rates, and is unpaid;
(b)	whenever the master, owner or person in charge of the vessel has infringed any provision of this act, or any by-law in force under this act, and has thereby rendered himself liable to a penalty.
In other words, that statute gives to the New Westminster harbour commission power to seize and detain a vessel, but there is no power to make a claim against the agent for damage that is done.
Then we come to the National Harbours Board Act as it stands at the present time. The section I am going to quote was the same as that in the act which set up the Vancouver harbour commission. The section in the act is section 16, which reads in this way:
The board-
That is the national harbours board.
-may, in the manner hereinafter set forth, seize and detain any vessel within the limits of the territorial waters of Canada in the following cases:-
Mind you, Mr. Chairman, this power of seizing and detaining a vessel is just about the most drastic power that can be exercised under our law.
- (a) whenever any sum is due in respect of the vessel for rates or tolls or for commuted rates or tolls and is unpaid;
(b) whenever the master, owner or person in charge of the vessel has violated or has failed to observe any provision of this act, or any by-law in force under this act, and has rendered himself liable to any penalty;-
That is the second ground on which the harbours board can seize.
- (c) whenever any injury has been done by the vessel or by the fault or neglect of the crew, while acting as the crew or under order of their superior officers, to any works or property under the administration, management and control of the board; or
(d) whenever any obstruction whatever has been offered or made to the operations of the board by any vessel or by the fault or neglect of the crew, while acting as the crew or under order of their superior officers.
We have those four provisions under which a vessel can be seized or detained. Then subsection 2 goes on to provide as follows:
In a case coming within paragraphs (c) or (d) of subsection (1) ...
That is, in only two of those four cases does subsection 2 apply, Then subsection 2 goes on to give a lien, to provide for selling and

so on. Then at the end of that subsection we find the portion which both the minister and the parliamentary assistant quoted this morning:
. . . the board has a preferential lien upon the vessel and upon the proceeds thereof until payment has been made or adequate security has been given for such damages, whether direct or indirect, and for the amount of all such injury, damages, expenses and costs as may be awarded in any suit resulting therefrom,-
Then we find these words:
-and the owner, charterer, master or agent of such vessel is also liable to the board for all such injury, damages, expenses and costs.
That provision only applies in the event of seizure under two of the four provisions for seizure. Furthermore, it obviously means that the board must first seize the ship, and that of course was the argument made by counsel for the Shipping Federation of Canada. In actual practice that is what has been done. I understand there has never been a case in which a claim has been brought against an agent. Why would there be? The board has the right to seize the vessel. Not only does it have the right to seize the vessel, but if we turn to section 15 of the National Harbours Board Act we find a provision that the customs official cannot let the vessel go out of the harbour until she has received a clearance from the national harbours board. Subsection 3 of that section reads as follows:
No officer of customs shall grant a clearance to any vessel to leave,
(a)	any harbour under the jurisdiction of the board until the master thereof produces to such officer of customs a certificate from an authorized officer of the board certifying that the rates or tolls on such vessel have been paid or that none are payable thereon or that in so far as the board is concerned a clearance may be granted-
In other words, no ship can leave the port of Vancouver until she produces to the customs officials a clearance from the national harbours board. Therefore it is impossible for a ship to get away if the national harbours board is not asleep. The subsection continues:
(b)	any other harbour or port in Canada-
That means any harbour that is not one of the seven national harbours.
-if he has been notified by the board to withhold such clearance until further notified by the board that in so far as the board is concerned a clearance may be granted.
It is no wonder that the provision about suing the agent has been a dead letter and that no action has ever been taken under it. No action should be taken either because the agent is in no way responsible for the operation of the vessel. Then we come to the bill. The minister and his parliamentary assistant both say that the new bill does not give the

board any wider powers, that it will have the same powers as it has had all along. If we turn to clause 8 of the bill, which contains a complete new section 16 for the National Harbours Board Act, we find in subsection 7 the following overriding provision:
Whether or not all or any of the rights of the board under this section are exercised by the board, the board may, in any case described in subsection (D -
I point out that there is an extension in itself. Subsection 1 contains six different provisions under which the board can seize a vessel, two of which are brand new and were not in the act before. But now the board is taking the power to claim against the agent in respect of the first two provisions, something they cannot do under the act as it stands at the present time. I continue:
-proceed against the owner of the vessel in any port of competent jurisdiction for the amount owing to the board, or for the balance thereof in the event of any sale contemplated by subsection (3), and may also exercise against the owner of the vessel any other right or remedy available to the board at law.
In that new subsection there is no suggestion at all that first recourse shall be had to the vessel. The board is taking the power to sue the agent right at the start. The board can let the vessel go out of the harbour and then sue the agent for any damage that is done by the vessel. It is no wonder that the shipping agents of Canada are upset about the provision. They cannot get insurance to cover damages of that kind, they cannot in fairness be asked to demand a bond from their shipping company, and in effect they are being put in a corner and made subject to a liability for which an agent should never be made liable..
I do repeat that the legislation should be restricted to the owner, the charterer by demise who has taken over the whole vessel, and the master. They are the people who can properly be made responsible for damage done by the vessel, but there is no right whatever to make the agent liable for that damage. I have here the brief which was submitted and I want to read the paragraph which points out that these agents are not agents in the accepted sense in ordinary business on shore. It reads as follows:
Section 1, subsection 1(e) (ea) which defines the owner as including the agent and charterer does not otherwise define what is meant by the words "agent" or "charterer" except as to the qualification that it is intended to mean the agent or charterer of the vessel. It is interesting to note as regards the agent, for instance, that the words used are not "the agent of the owner", but "the agent of the vessel"; therefore it is quite clear that reference is had to what is known in common parlance as "vessels' agents" or as "husbanding agents".
National Harbours Board Act Vessels' agents or husbanding agents are not in any sense of the word the representatives of the owners of the vessel. They are simply co-ordinators of services and will, for a modest fee, provide certain services to vessels coming into a port to load and discharge cargo. They will act as agents de liaison between the master of the vessel and the stevedores who will load and discharge the vessel, the ship chandlers who will replenish her stores, the coal or oil merchant who will fill her bunkers, the shipping master who will sign off or sign on her crew, the customs officer who will grant a certificate of clearance, the tug owner who will provide towing services in and out of berth, the pilotage authority who will provide the pilot to take the vessel out to sea.
Agents who do work of that kind should not be made liable for damage by the vessel to the harbours board property. Yet with the new subsection 7 of section 16 these agents will be primarily liable for all such damage. It is to remedy that difficulty that I have moved that the word "agent" be deleted from the definition of "owner". The harbours board will still have the complete right to seize and detain the vessel and to prevent the customs people giving clearance. It still has complete rights against the owner, the charterer by demise and the master; but why drag the poor agent into this liability?

Our Minister of Transport has introduced a bill to protect the taxpayers' money, and there was no one in the opposition who suggested that by this bill the board could collect money that did not belong to the taxpayers of this country. If any owner, agent or master was in control of a ship that damaged the harbour, certainly someone should pay. We as members supporting the government are anxious to see that the taxpayers' money, the money of the people whom we represent and the people who charged us with the responsibility of taking care of their assets, should be protected. Now, Mr. Chairman, there is another objection to this clause, paragraph (d). In the committee changes were made to (b) and (c) which had the effect of taking away the direct responsibility of the owner and placing it on the vessel itself. But here


in (d) we still have the word "owner" which, of course, includes the agent. Paragraph (d) is as follows:
The board may, as provided in section 18, seize any vessel within the territorial waters of Canada in any case where . . .
(d) the owner of the vessel has in respect of the vessel committed an offence under this act or the by-laws, punishable upon summary conviction by a penalty payable under section 21 to the board.
The fact about that paragraph which should be noted is that it gives the board the right to seize a vessel before there has been any proof of breach of the bylaws. It can be seized before there has been any proof that the bylaws have been broken.
The maximum fine for breaking a bylaw is $500, so that the board is trying to get in the position where it can seize and detain a vessel although there may or may not be a breach of the bylaw for which the total penalty would be only $500. Because the agent is covered by the definition of owner, the board can also seize the vessel where it is thought that the agent has broken a bylaw, let alone the owner having broken a bylaw or the vessel having broken it. There is a provision in paragraph (f) for seizure where there has been a conviction for breaking a bylaw. That surely should be enough if a bylaw has actually been broken and it has been proved to be broken. Then, I suppose one could not quarrel so much with the power of seizure. Surely there should not be the power of seizure of a vessel where there may or may not have been a breach of a bylaw and the maximum penalty is only $500.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lionel Chevrier (Minister of Transport) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PROVISION FOR REGULATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL HIGHWAY TRANSPORT
speechtext:
for leave to introduce Bill No. 474, respecting extra-provincial motor vehicle transport.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I would like to make an explanatory statement to the house on introducing this bill. The judgment of the privy council in the Winner case decided that the federal parliament has exclusive jurisdiction over interprovincial and international transportation undertakings. This jurisdiction extends not only to undertakings engaged in transport of goods or passengers between provinces, or between a province and another country, but also covers traffic movements within the province which are carried on as a part of an interprovincial or international undertaking.
Although such undertakings are subject to certain provincial laws of application, it appears that only parliament can legislate with respect to such matters as the granting of licences and the fixing of rates. It follows that federal legislation is required before control can be exercised by the province.
The purpose of this bill, therefore, is to enable provincial administrations to exercise control within each province over interprovincial and international highway transport undertaking. This would place the provinces in much the same position as before the decision of the courts in the Winner case. The act would come into force in a province by proclamation as and when that province is ready to operate under its terms.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, this bill is the result of the resolution which has been passed and I would like to make a few general comments on it. Hon. members will recall from the budget that the tax reductions this year which, I ventured to say at the time, you could put in your eye, are practically all contained in the Excise Tax Act. I shall not take up the time of the house at any length in dealing with this but I think we should remind ourselves of one or two things which, although they have been said again and again, require to be repeated.
We should remind ourselves of the extent of the hidden taxes which pyramid and which hurt the individual and which also put up the costs of all those who are manufacturing. We should remind ourselves that these high taxes have now produced a vicious circle so that we are finding it harder to sell abroad. We should remind ourselves that unemployment marches on and that the government has had very little to say about how it is to be dealt with.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) suggested that businessmen sharpen their pencils and figure out how they can reduce costs, but it would have been much more practical if some of the taxes could have been reduced. At the same time the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), as reported at page 2106 of Hansard, rather blithely suggested this was the year to loosen up the purse strings, in other words it was not a year for economy. As a result of those and other things we now find disturbing signs, and we have had them for some time, in the textile industry. We have also seen them in the electrical manufacturing industry, and now we have disturbing news from the motorcar industry of substantial layoffs on the part of some of the larger manufacturers.
As the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) pointed out in his speech, the minister seemed to be interested only in two or three-wheeled vehicles and to have nothing whatever to offer as regards four-wheeled vehicles. In other words, no reduction was made in the huge tax on motorcars and we can, I think, very easily attribute the present layoffs, which are disturbing, and which perhaps will be more disturbing, to the fact that there has been no reduction on motorcars.
Excise Tax Act
Prices are high and therefore we have distress cropping up in the motor industry as well as in the textile and electrical appliances industries.
When we come more to the details of this bill it is hard to see why some of the articles were selected at all. In fact, it seems as though the minister was in a very lighthearted mood when he made the selection. We have firearms, golf clubs, fishing reels, cameras, ash trays, tires, and tubes. Tires and tubes are more practical and more important. However, it almost looks as though the minister had been in rather a light-hearted mood, or perhaps had thought that, as there was such a small reduction anyway, it did not matter much where it was put, and that one place would be as good as another.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is necessary for me to take up more of the time of the house. We now have this bill implementing what was set out in the budget resolutions. The matter was debated at that time. I shall not now take up more of the time of the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) has just pointed out, this is one of the bills that implement the budget proposals made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on April 6. We feel that this bill points up the fact that the minister took the taxes off in the wrong places. This bill specifically indicates that on a certain number of luxury goods there is to be a reduction in taxes but that, as for the general sales tax across the board, which should have been reduced, no effort was made by the government to make any reduction in that direction. We therefore look upon this measure as another one of those bills that reduce the taxes in the wrong places, without cutting taxes that should have been reduced.

Speaker, I do not wish to prolong the discussion but inasmuch as I did not have an opportunity of saying anything with regard to the budget, I want to say a few words with respect to this bill.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) has stated that the unemployment situation is serious. Today an announcement was made by the wheat board to the effect that the sales price of wheat had been reduced by some ten cents a bushel, a fact which indicates a serious situation in the marketing of the products of this country and one that deserves the serious attention of the house, late though it is in the session. The hon. member for Greenwood

Excise Tax Act
referred to the unemployment situation as being somewhat intensified in recent days in the automobile industry, and the hon. member who just took his seat stated that the reductions which were made in taxation this year were reductions on those things that did not seriously affect the economy of the people. There still remain the hidden taxes on the needs of the home, including furniture, clothing, boots and shoes and the like. The reductions on those things on which they were made represent but little saving for the average man or woman in this country.
In the last few days particular attention has been given to the automobile industry. In view of the fall-away in the purchase of and the demand for automobiles and the fact that the tremendous taxes levied on automobiles have been responsible for the reduction in that demand, I suggest that consideration should be given, even at this late date, to bringing in legislation which would reduce the excise and other taxes that are levied on automobiles today, in order to meet the threatening and rising unemployment situation.
One does not want to go back to 1929; one does not want to recall those days; but, in considering the events of today, one cannot lose sight of the fact that during 1929 unemployment was touching industries similar to those which are affected today. In 1929 we had a tremendous bumper crop of wheat, as we had in 1928. No action was taken then when action should have been taken. Even as late as February, 1930, in the speech from the throne of that year, the governor general had words placed in his mouth to the effect that Canada was in an exceptionally fine position, for no part of the 1929 wheat crop had been sold. Today we are in the same position as far as the 1953 crop is concerned. I feel that even now, in these late days of the session, serious consideration should be given by the government to doing something to meet not only the agricultural situation but generally the threatening and rising unemployment problem which must be met and which can only be met now in advance of a possibly more serious situation developing in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a word with regard to this bill. Under it no relief, or practically none, is given to the Canadian manufacturer of watches and clocks. The excise tax has been reduced by only 5 per cent, leaving a 10 per cent excise on watches and clocks except those for use of railway men and the blind. This leaves a 10 per cent

excise tax; and on top of that we have the 10 per cent sales tax. These taxes result in a tremendous handicap to the Canadian manufacturer. On top of that, watch parts and watches are allowed into this country under an extremely low duty-what you might call a dumping duty-which does not give the Canadian manufacturer or the Canadian worker a chance to compete. I personally feel-as I know do those in the business -that this excise tax on clocks and watches certainly should be taken off altogether. Clocks and watches are not luxury items; they are a necessity. A worker has to have a clock in order to know when to get up to go to work, so that he may work all during the day and the week. At the end of the week he gets his pay cheque but his taxes are deducted. I do not think you should charge that man twice; and that is what is being done.

I should like to ask the
parliamentary assistant the meaning of this section. I do so because if I read it correctly the clause, while on the face of it appearing to fix the period of limitation at three years for summary conviction matters, in addition provides that action can be taken alternatively within one year from the date on which evidence, sufficient in the opinion of the minister to justify a prosecution for the offence, came to his knowledge. That would seem to extend the period of prosecution almost synonymously with eternity. As I see it, if the crown were in the position at the end of three years that it had no action or in its opinion could not successfully take proceedings, it could extend the investigation indefinitely until such time as the minister signified by a simple certificate that within one year of a certain date sufficient evidence had been secured or was in process of being secured, and therefore action could now be taken.
I must say that is not what one would call a limitation section. If my interpretation is correct, and I am merely submitting it to the parliamentary assistant for his consideration, it is actually a delimitation section, with the period limited only to within one year from the date on which the minister signs a certificate that evidence has come to his knowledge which in his opinion is sufficient upon which to found a prosecution. I think the essence of our law, even for the most serious offences, is that there must be a limitation to the taking of proceedings at some time.
In the case of murder, for instance, as I recall it, the person must die within one year and one day of the wrongful acts. While I wish to see every assistance given to the department to punish fraud and wrongdoing, surely the books of prosecution should not be open indefinitely as they will be under this clause when proceedings will be conditional and upon the prerequisite that the minister signs a certificate that information has finally come to the department within one year of which prosecution can take place.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The only difference between this proposal and the present act is the extension frem six months to one year for the minister to have the opportunity to get his auditors' reports and for the person involved to have the opportunity to answer the minister. There they have a five-year period instead of three years, but they also have the twelve-month period instead of six months, and it has been found that it is necessary.

With deference to the hon. member, I point out that it is not quite as simple as that. The present section reads in part as follows:
. . . but where false or fraudulent acts . . . are involved in any offence committed . . . the prosecution or suit may be commenced at any time within the said period of three years or within six months after the minister or the deputy minister of national revenue for customs and excise has knowledge or notice of such false or fraudulent acts . . .

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

That does not answer the situation at all. The hon. gentleman says the only change we have made is to extend the present six months' period following the three years to one year, but that is not the only change. The only reason for the three years not being the final period of limitation previously was in a case where there had been fraud or fraudulent acts. I can understand the arguments of my hon. friend that the auditors are far behind and that there should be an additional six months provided in order to meet the wrongdoing of fraudulent individuals. But surely where there has not been fraud the individual should not be placed in a position where, no matter how long after the alleged offence, he could find himself in a position where he is subject to a prosecution. That is not the principle of the law. The principle of law is that a period of limitation should ordinarily be provided.
The minister says that the earlier provision is in effect in the Income Tax Act, if I heard him correctly. Would he read the corresponding section of the Income Tax Act?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I made on the resolution stage quite a full explanation of the proposal in this budget to change the method of taxing beer from a malt basis to a gallonage basis. My remarks appear at page 4835 of Hansard for May 18, 1954. Most of the changes in this act are consequent upon that change in the method of taxation.
Subsection 1 of section 1 of this bill proposes the removal from the act of marking provisions which it is felt would be better issued as regulations. This section 171 has been in the act for the last 15 or 20 years, but has been outdated by the change in the production methods of the modern breweries, as well as new methods of marketing and distribution by interlocking arrangements or reciprocal agreements. To meet these changes, it is desired to adopt labelling requirements similar to those which have been in effect for distilleries for some time and which have worked out very satisfactorily for comparable conditions.
Under section 176 of the act-which it will be seen is also being amended by section 3 of this bill-the governor in council is empowered to make such regulations as are necessary for the carrying into effect and the enforcement of the provisions of the act, and it is considered that this authority should be extended to provide for the prescribing of regulations for the marking of containers.

Am I correct in understanding that the substance of this is that there be two methods of taxing, one by gallonage and the other by poundage, and that this is really designed to remove any discrimination by applying only one method?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The substance of the bill is that we adopt the gallonage method. It changes the schedules, establishing new
Excise Act
methods for taxing on a basis of gallonage, rather than the system we have had hitherto of taxing on a poundage basis, on the malt.

Then we can take it that this bill, which seems to have a rather large number of sections to achieve a simple purpose, is to make the necessary technical changes to give effect to what the parliamentary assistant has just said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: With the exception of the labelling regulation, that is correct.
Does the parliamentary assistant expect to get in more revenue in this way?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I explained at the resolution stage that the gallonage rate seems to be approximately the rate that was effective on the malt. I explained that when the original tax on a poundage basis was established the brewers were putting about two pounds of malt to a gallon of beer. We have found that under efficient manufacturing methods that has been becoming somewhat less. I believe it is down to roughly 1 [DOT] 8 pounds per gallon of beer. We think that the tax revenue will be about the same, with the exception I indicated that there would be an effective reduction in the rate on about 6 per cent of the beer that is brewed, which is manufactured from corn flakes and corn adjuncts. But the agricultural community felt that we were taxing them unfairly on the beer in relation to the product made from malt.

I wanted to say a word or two on clause 3, with reference to schedule B, on the principle of the drawback, which is to be found on page 11 of the bill, item 1044. That item sets out that fire clay or fire brick imported into Canada for certain purposes is subject to a duty, but that duty is wiped out by permitting a 99 per cent drawback of the duty if the material is imported for those purposes. I consider that that drawback, even in those particular cases, retards and militates against the development of industry of that kind in Canada. I do not see very much sense in importing fire brick or fire clay from the United States and putting a tariff against it and then permitting a 99 per cent drawback on the material, which in effect nullifies the tariff. In my judgment that principle prevents the development of an industry of the type that we are dealing with.
I point out also that that same principle militates against the maintenance and the development of a coal industry in this country. Coal is facing a crisis, and this drawback on coal imported from the United States and used for metallurgical purposes is a principle that is preventing the expansion and maintenance of a coal industry in this country. For a great many years there has been a duty of 50 cents a ton on bituminous coal from the United States; but coal imported from the United States has a drawback of 99 per cent, which means that on all coal imported and used in Canada for metallurgical purposes the tariff is wiped out because of the drawback.
I disagree completely with that principle. If we are going to put on a tariff, then the tariff should be applied without the device that is now being used, as indicated by this part of the schedule B. There would be very little difficulty in developing a fire clay or a fire brick industry in this country. There is a substantial fire clay and fire brick industry in Canada at the present time, particularly in the maritime provinces. The device of a drawback or a refund of the tariff put on at the border, in my opinion, is a bad principle, and it injures the development and expansion of industry in this country, I do not care what industry it is. I know it has militated greatly against the best interests of the coal industry in this country, and I would suggest to the parliamentary assistant-I know he cannot do anything about it now-that this
Income Tax Act
matter should be taken under the consideration of the Department of Finance with the end in view of arriving at some other arrangement that would not put in the stop-blocks that this device puts against the development of industry in Canada.

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 467, to amend the Income Tax Act.

I want to make one or two general observations, Mr. Speaker. The Income Tax Act has now invaded the lives of almost everybody and is a matter of great importance to them. It seems to me a great pity that a matter which is infinitely complicated in itself seems almost more complicated by what on the face of it looks like a multiplication of statutes.
We have the Income War Tax Act; we have the Income Tax Act and then we have The Income Tax Act. These last two are extraordinarily difficult to keep separate because sometimes the "the's" get spelled with small letters instead of capital letters. I suppose it is obvious to say it is desirable that legislation should be clear, simple, definite and unequivocal.
As I said a moment ago, the subject matter here is extraordinarily complicated. I would ask the minister whether it is not possible that even further efforts might be made to simplify the situation. Will it eventually work out so that these three will not be necessary? I understand there are certain temporary features which make it hard to

Income Tax Act
deal with the situation at the moment, but it seems to me that at the present time it is a little like the antediluvian method of dealing with land titles when people had to carry the title deeds around with them in a box, otherwise they could not make a title to then-property. After that we got registration deeds and that, of course, led eventually to the land title system wherein they adopted the method we now have of dealing with ships and applied it to land.
I am not going to belabour the point but I would just ask the minister whether there is any hope that we might work out a simpler method. I am quite sure he will agree that almost anyone whose affairs are in the least bit complicated must obtain outside assistance, although I admit the Department of National Revenue does a good deal to help. Nevertheless it is still true that anyone whose affairs are complicated must obtain legal advice and, as a matter of fact, there are actually only a minority of lawyers who have mastered the intricacies of the whole act. I suppose it would be a sad day for them if things became too simple, but I imagine that even after simplification there would be plenty of difficulties with which they can deal.
I know it is difficult but I would like to submit to the minister that the problem still remains of doing something to make this complicated situation seem less complicated and somewhat more clear than it is now.
