Mr. Speaker, my subject deals with the question of taxation on savings for pension purposes. I raised the issue on the resolution stage when the minister was not present, though a brief reply was given to the point I endeavoured to make at that time. Since then I have taken the trouble to study with some care the answers given by the minister to some of the same problems last year.

Now, Mr. Speaker, what we are being asked to do in this bill is to increase the exemption allowed to people who are employed in regard to the contribution which they make to approved pension funds. The exemptions covered in the act extend to $900 for employees' contribution, and $900 for the employer's contribution, which is a total contribution to the pension fund of $1,800. With respect to arrears, I understand in this case the employee, if he so wishes, can pay another $900 and the employer an additional $900 making a total of $1,800, or $3,600 in all which is the amount of earnings which will be exempt from tax in the case of an employed person.
As I understand the present bill, the $900 contribution in each case is increased to $1,500, which means that a total of $6,000 of the earnings of an employed person can be put aside into a pension fund and thus be exempt from tax. For a man to be able to save that much money, after paying living expenses and meeting other taxes, I estimate that his tax bracket would have to be in the neighbourhood of 47J or 50 per cent, so that, in effect, in the case of an employed person the government is contributing half the money that that person saves and puts into a pension fund.
Now, I would like to say a few words about the views expressed by the minister last year, because I have not been convinced by what was said this year, nor by reading last year's debate, that the self-employed person is in any different position from that of the employed person. I hope the minister himself, who has always expressed some doubt or at least some concern on this point, will in time accept the argument that has been advanced by a good many people and which affects a great many people in this country.
The number of people who paid income tax in the self-employed class during the last full year for which tax statistics are available was 319,000; they are made up of primary producers, professional men, business proprietors and financial people. Those
319,000	taxpayers represent a fairly good cross-section of the industry of the country. I may say right now that the income tax they paid was $246 million in 1951. In other words, 320,000 people paid $246 million of income tax as against $543 million income tax paid by employees who are now entitled to the benefits of the tax-free saving which is allowed to those who contribute to pension funds. In other words, the amount of tax paid in the case of the self-employed was half as much as that paid by the employees. Yet the deductions which those self-employed 83276-354
Income Tax Act
people were allowed to make for their savings paid into pension funds was only 4 mills on the tax dollar paid by them. Four mills on the tax dollar was the total extent of the pension deduction made by that class of people. The employed, on the other hand, averaged 20 cents in pension deductions on every tax dollar paid by them. There is therefore a great disparity between the position of the two groups. Unless the minister and the government are thoroughly satisfied that that disparity is not unfair, I suggest that it is not too late even yet to find a means of dealing with this problem.
May I deal briefly with the points which the minister made last year. In the first place he said that this system of allowing deductions for the savings made by people during their earning years was a departure in principle from the general principle of the act, that new principle being that there is a tax postponement given on savings devoted to the purchase of retirement annuities. The adoption of this principle followed the Ives commission report which advocated a uniform system of taxing pension income when it is received as a pension and not when the money is put into the fund as a saving. That procedure has the effect of freeing from tax the income as it is earned and put into the fund but makes it taxable after retirement when that income is paid back to the pensioner in the form of his pension.
Obviously there is a great disparity in the rate of tax paid by a man who is at the height of his earning powers and is making his best salary in his middle years and the rate of tax which he will pay on a relatively small pension after he has retired. The consequence is that you are treating one class of people in one way and are treating another class of people in a different way. In other words, to ask the self-employed to pay a tax on their earnings when they are at the height of their earning capacity and then to be relatively free when that pension eventually becomes payable after they are retired and when their income is small is quite unfair, in my opinion.
The minister explained the advantage of this method. He said that it was a principle that was a departure in the first instance. But, the principle having been adopted, he found there was considerable mechanical difficulty in applying it further and going beyond the case of employed persons. As I understand the proposition, that argument simply comes down to the statement that the mechanics of tax convenience stand in the way of treating the self-employed person in the same way as the employed person is treated. I suggest to this honourable house

Income Tax Act
that that is not an answer for what is obviously a disparity or a discrimination between the two groups.
The second point that was made is that the government is interested in seeing pension plans adopted in industry. However, it does not agree that because employees have tax postponement, therefore self-employed persons should likewise have it in respect of their voluntary savings. Mr. Speaker, if saving for a pension is good for a Canadian because he is employed and paid by another, why is not saving for a pension equally good for his neighbour who makes his own living? Why call the saving of one person voluntary and the saving of the other person involuntary or something different in kind?
The third point was that the self-employed can buy endowment policies or annuities and that he receives very reasonable tax treatment. I agree that that is the case. After he has paid his tax on his income, if he has any left with which to buy an annuity, he can buy an annuity on favourable terms as to tax. But that is not really the dispute at all in this case. The question is whether he should be allowed to buy his annuity before he has paid his tax.
The fourth point was that an employee's savings are locked up in an approved pension plan. That is quite true, although I suggest that it is no more true than it would be in the case of self-employed persons if the approved annuity plans in which they could invest were not subject to anticipation. As I see it, the minister's point is that when an employed person makes his contribution into the firm's pension fund he has no right to withdraw it during the course of his employment or, in fact, until he reaches a certain age. I believe there are a great many exceptions to that provision. I myself know of some in my own experience. I refer to those who leave employment after a period of time, even under these approved plans, and withdraw the capital from the fund. However, that is by the way. The point is that the savings of a self-employed person could equally well be tied up by annuity plans which could not be anticipated. I see no insuperable technical problem in that matter. I am sure that the insurance company annuities and the government annuities could be written in terms which would prevent anticipation of the fund, except in certain emergency cases which would be so minor as not to affect the principal.
The fifth point which the minister made was that if this benefit or principle or policy of encouraging savings for old age pensions were extended beyond employees, there would be no logical stopping point short of
fMr. Michener. J
allowing this privilege to everybody, including employees not now covered by pension plans. To that argument I say "Quite so". There is and there should be no stopping point short of every person who is earning enough money to save some of it for a pension or annuity against the time when he will have to retire.
Those who are not working for firms which have had the initiative to instal pension plans are unable to get the benefit that accrues to their neighbours in an adjoining plant where there is an approved pension plan in effect. In two plants on the same street you will find that the employees are affected differently. The employee is not responsible for that condition. It is his employer who in the one case has not seen fit to instal a pension plan. As the law stands, the employee can do nothing about it. If the minister would accept my proposition and approve certain types of annuities which are the equivalent to pensions the employee whose firm did not see fit to have a plan could still make his savings, provide for his retirement and obtain his exemption just as the other employee does.
The sixth point made by the minister was that he did not know what volume of savings would be attracted. He thought that a substantial sum might be involved. I think that is so. The amount might be substantial, and I will come to the actual amount in a few minutes when I deal with the minister's next point which I give in his own words as follows:
I am not sure that at this stage of Canadas development I would like to take the responsibility for directing the savings of the Canadian people away from equities into debt securities.
What that means is, as I understand it, that if the 320,000 self-employed who now pay taxes saved $240 on an average, basing the amount on the rate of savings of a member of parliament under the parliamentary pension fund, the amount of savings which would be tax exempt would be only $76 million. To say that the economy of Canada is going to be thrown off balance or that our capital investment program is going to be upset by an amount of $76 million, and that that it is a serious matter for the government seems to me to be illogical and unrealistic. I think the minister was probably reaching for arguments at that point to satisfy the department because obviously they do not wish to undertake to deal with the problem owing to the mechanical difficulties.
It seems to me that the argument that it would seriously affect the investment balance as between equity and debt securities is quite a long shot as an answer to this serious

discrimination. Surely if the investment policy of the country is involved tax policy can act more directly to secure investment in equities as the minister has done with his very creditable arrangement for allowing deductions from tax with respect to dividends. Surely it could be done much more effectively that way than by making fish out of the self-employed and budget birds out of the employed.

The minister's concern seems to be that those who are self-employed should be required to risk their capital in equity investment instead of saving it for their retirement but those who have security of employment with a firm paying their salaries are not subject to the same concern. What he says in effect is that these employed chaps had better be careful, that they had better save for their old age and the department will not now tax the money they are receiving in the pension fund which is going into gilt-edge securities. On the other hand, he says that the people who do not have the security of a steady job and who are working at their own risk had better risk their savings as well if they have any after paying income tax. He says that he thinks that they should not save anything that has not been fully taxed even if it goes into an approved form of annuity that is payable and taxable when the person is too old to work.
May I refer again to the figures as to the amounts and number of people involved. They are the best I could find. As I said before, there are about 320,000 self-employed who pay income tax. They are divided into a great many different categories. I shall not repeat the instances which I gave in my earlier remarks. I think perhaps one of the most cogent instances is the case of a nurse who is employed by a hospital working alongside a nurse who is working for a patient by the day.

which they paid a tax of $23 million. These statistics show how much of that total taxable income was allowed as a deduction by reason of being paid into a pension fund. When we come to the professional group, which includes many hon. members in the house, taxable income amounted to $158 million, and the total amount which was allowed to be saved tax free was $227,000. I come to the amount of the exemption allowed to the employed simply because they were employed and not on any other basis of distinction. They earned and received the same kind of dollars, and the only principle of differentiation was that in the one case they were paid by an employer's cheque and in the other case the money was earned by some kind of trade or activity. The amount that was allowed by way of exemption to the employed in the same period was $95 million, which was 100 times as much as the amount allowed to the self-employed. That is out of all proportion, of course, to the numbers in these two representative groups. The number of employees was 2,444,000, which is perhaps eight times as many as the self-employed.
As I said before the principle involved appears to me to come down simply to one of the method of receiving one's remuneration for one's activity in the commercial life of the country. I do urge the minister to review this situation again, and I would be glad to suggest to him a very simple amendment to the act which would make it possible for the department to approve pension fund or annuity payments, which have the same features as approved pension plans now for industry. In this way a great number of people throughout the country who wish to provide for their old age, or for the time when they must retire, can do so on the same terms as those who are employed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I should like to say a word while we are discussing the amendments to the Income Tax Act. There are two points that I should like to mention. One case concerns a father who is able to send a young boy or girl through school to enter a profession or to be a high school teacher. After the child reaches the age of 16 the deduction of $150 is no longer permitted from income tax and the family allowance payments are stopped. If the child is continuing in school, the parent is able to claim $400 per year deduction from income tax. I approve of that very strongly.
However, then we have the case of another boy or girl whose parents are not able to send them on to school in the manner of the first parent I mentioned. In this case the boy or girl struggles to get through school, then takes a six weeks' course at Toronto and spends one year as a teacher. Then, this young person may return to normal school and endeavour, by means of summer courses, to improve his situation until he eventually gets his B.A. and becomes a high school teacher. My feeling is that such a young man or young woman should be able to claim the tuition fees and the amount spent for books for these summer courses as a deduction from income tax.
My own feeling is that boy or girl is endeavouring to improve his or her situation and improve the standards of the profession which he or she decides upon. The income tax department will receive more in taxes because that boy or girl made that improvement, and consequently receives higher wages.
There is another class to which I shall refer, and with respect to whom I should like to see a clarification of the act. I refer to the young farm boy who stays on the farm. This young boy has completed perhaps two or three years of high school, and returns to the farm at 15 or 16 years of age. The family allowance payments are stopped and the father is not able to claim any reduction from his income tax because the boy no longer attends school. The father enters into an agreement with the boy, verbally I will admit, by means of which the boy agrees to stay on the farm without wages until such time as he is ready to be married when the father will supply him with a farm.
When the farm is passed over to the boy at the age of 26 or 27, the income tax department steps in and says, "You have received $10,000 in this year and you must pay income tax on the amount." Now, that is unfair to this young man. He has worked for some 10 or 12 years without wages in order that he may receive the farm, and to be

taxed on that amount in one year is unfair. The boy would have no objection to having the amount spread over the period when he was working on the farm, and he is quite willing to pay income tax on that. It is unfair when he works all those years without wages and then when he receives the farm in lieu of wages to be faced with all that tax in one year. I should like the Minister of Finance to endeavour to clarify that in the interests of these young farm boys.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I had planned to do that as soon as we got into committee. It is quite true that the Income Tax Act is complex. It always has been, and as a matter of fact it perhaps becomes a little more complex each year. The reason for that, as I have had occasion to say several times, is an endeavour to introduce various relief provisions into the act. It is found from experience that certain exemptions are desirable, certain special cases need to be taken care of, and provision is made in the law for them. You will find a number of examples of that in the bill which is now before the committee. A great many of these are rather minor in character, but they are of a relief nature. Some of them have been suggested by members of parliament, some by the bar association, some by accountants associations, and so on.
There are three acts referred to here, it is true. You have the principal act and that is the, with a small "t", Income Tax Act. The Income War Tax Act must continue in force as long as there are taxes to which it applies. The other is The, with a capital "T", Income Tax Act, and that is really a transitional measure that operated from the period 1949 to 1952. I repeat that the reason for the apparent complexity of this statute is a genuine desire to ensure that the charging provisions are as fairly and equitably applied as possible.
The simplest kind of income tax act would be just to put a flat rate or a progressive rate of tax on people's income, without any exemptions or deductions, but that would be manifestly unfair. The complexity is due almost entirely to the deductions, the exemptions, the relief provisions, the exceptions and so on. I should like to say that it will become simpler in future years but I just do not believe it will.
I suppose there are also, in addition to the relief sections, the sections that work in the opposite direction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The ones to which I euphemistically refer as the loophole sections.

I wanted to say that one quite realizes the complexity of this act. I have glanced rather quickly over the bill, and I think that although the minister may say the great majority are minor and probably the great majority are for relief, yet there are about 50 amendments to the various Clauses and subsections of these various acts. It does seem to me that a bill that is as complex as that should not be delayed until May 31 before receiving first reading and having the bill distributed to the members of this house. There are quite a few competent accountants in this house, and I would say we have some lawyers who have tried to earn a living by interpreting this and similar acts. I am quite sure if any one of them had taken this bill when it first came into the house and spent all the available time, except for meal hours, they would just about now have been able to arrive at some intelligent approximation of what all these sections mean. Because, when you read one clause you find that it says, perhaps, "save and except for subsection 2 of paragraph (w) of clause 4 of section 97"- and when you go there you find that you end up with everything except the Acts of the Apostles and the beatitudes-and anything else that can be thrown in, just for good measure.
The minister brings in his bill at this time. Of course we accept his statement, because he is always so frank with the house, and so good-natured. He just smiles and says, "This is all right". Sometimes I think he has been impressed by one of his parliamentary predecessors who at one time is supposed to have said, "Hold the legislation back until the hot weather comes along, and it will drive the boys home." Well, we have not had any hot weather, but time is getting on. I am simply saying that I do think a bill like this could have been brought in earlier in the session, so that those who have had some experience in dealing with these matters could have done something about it.

The $5,000 expended for repairing the building is an expense, so that there is no income tax payable. One amount offsets the other. But if the $5,000 is received and only $3,000 is spent, there will be a recapture to the extent of $2,000.
With due respect to the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, this section is merely putting in clear form what has been the recognized and existing practice in the department.
What is the "reasonable time" to which reference is made in clause l(lXii)?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We had a great many representations on this. I cannot recall offhand who in particular asked for it, but it is an amendment which has my complete support. I believe in a steeply progressive income tax, and I support the principle that a deduction may be made in the case of approved pension plans of the contributions made by the employer and the employee. The figure of $900 was established some years ago prior to what we all recognize as being a very substantial rise in the general level of prices. If $900 was fair 5 years or 10 years ago, then a somewhat higher figure is fair today. Let me say this at once. I believe that we should be as fair to people of moderate or high income as we are to people of low income. The basis of our Income Tax Act is, as I say, a steeply progressive tax where your high bracket income taxpayer pays a very substantial portion of his income back in the form of taxes, and I support that. But I see no reason why one should not be equally fair in a tax provision to that class of taxpayer as any other.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I remember when the $900 figure was written into the statute, and as I recall I made no objection to it at the time. But it did seem to me it was a pretty generous provision to make, bearing in mind the amount of pension that one can buy if he is in a position to pay $900 into a fund, and if that $900 can be matched by $900 from the employer. Everyone knows the provisions of the pension plan to which members of parliament contribute. We are paying in only $240 a year, and if we are here long enough it is possible, on the basis of that amount per year, plus the money which is put in by the government and the interest put into the fund, for a member of parliament to obtain a pension of $3,000 a year.
When you start to talk about contributions of $900 a year, matched by another $900, you can readily see, without bothering to go into the kind of figures I gave earlier, that you are talking about a much higher pension. My point is that the $900 ceiling was higher than it needed to be in 1946. It may be that we should have objected to it then so that we would not have this argument thrown at us now. But that being the case, I certainly do not think it is necessary to raise this ceiling to $1,500.
As the hon. member for St. Paul's has pointed out, it is possible in some instances for a total amount of $6,000 in the course of a year to be made income tax deductible in the case of one person. That would be $3,000

Income Tax Act
from the employee and $3,000 from the employer. The kind of employees I know best are not making enough that that kind of money could be deducted in the course of a year for pension purposes. But the point is, as the hon. member for St. Paul's pointed out, that anyone whose pension contributions are of that size is up in an income tax bracket where there is quite a substantial saving because of the percentage that applies to his top increment of income. It does seem to me that this is going a little too high, bearing in mind, as I say, the fact that $900 is being changed to $1,500 in four places.
I think there are some flaws which the minister might point out in the argument put forward by the hon. member for St. Paul's. But generally I agree with the position the hon. member took that we should be extending this provision on a horizontal basis, taking in more people, rather than extending it on a vertical basis as the minister is doing in this provision of this bill. I still wish he could be more specific as to who asked for this change.

Before the clause carries I want to support what my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, has said. This is a provision that is pretty difficult for us to justify with a serious face. We were trying to get some information from the parliamentary assistant as to how much this was going to cost taxpayers. The parliamentary assistant was not able to answer that question. While the total probably is not large, it is going to give assistance to people who are in very high income brackets and who in my opinion do not need assistance. I wonder whether the minister can now give us some estimate as to how much this proposed change is going to cost the treasury of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed it is really almost impossible to give an accurate estimate of what this will cost. It would not be substantial, of course, because my hon. friend is quite right. There is a relatively small number of people who would be benefited by the amendment. It is only the people who have the somewhat larger incomes, and therefore would be able to pay in the larger amount. But, as I say, I can see no difference in principle between giving that kind of man fair treatment and giving it to the larger mass who have not that size of an income.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is a question of what is fair. We think this goes too far.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend may argue that it was not fair in the first place. But, as he himself said, he did not protest it at that time.

I have not any quarrel with the clause in so far as it deals with employees except, as has been said, it seems to be giving relief upwards instead of horizontally, as I have argued for. This would be the appropriate place for an amendment, Mr. Chairman. I am saying simply as to that that there is not a very difficult technical problem involved in making the change which I have suggested. If the minister would accept the idea, it might be dealt with in general terms and left for regulation because it seems to me it is largely a mechanical problem in the department to determine proportionately what sort of savings a small businessman or a man who is self-employed, professional and other groups that I call self-employed, should be allowed to make which would be equivalent to an approved pension fund that their fellows in the employed class are making. I appreciate there is probably an administrative problem there, but it does not seem to me at all insuperable and I do urge that the effort be made.
I have an amendment here, Mr. Chairman, which I am not going to move now but I would submit it for the consideration of the minister. If the minister has made up his mind that this is something which cannot be dealt with now I certainly would not wish to urge it upon him for immediate decision because I know that there are difficulties involved. My suggested amendment deals with subsection 5 of section 2 of the bill. It amends sections in the act which now deal with employees. The addition which I suggest would deal with the taxpayer generally and the whole section would read:
"The following amounts may be deducted in computing the income tax of a taxpayer for the taxation year.
(i) The amount contributed by a taxpayer under an approved superannuation fund or plan . . .
(iii) Not exceeding $3,000 paid in the year by a self-employed taxpayer for or on account of the purchase for himself of an approved retirement annuity or pension as defined by the regulations."
If that phraseology were not broad enough it might be extended to include superannuation fund or plan, or approved annuity or pension plan, and then would follow the suggested third paragraph set out above.
The $3,000 I suggest as being a comparable figure because an employed person has a possibility of saving $3,000 which will not be taxed. The $1,500 of salary he receives and the $1,500 the employer contributes are all part of the man's salary because no employer would contribute to a pension fund an amount which his employee is not earning.

I am aware this would not solve the problem entirely but it leaves it open if the minister is so disposed to tackle it and it would perhaps assist him in working out a solution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a problem with which, as some hon. members know, I have been struggling for seven or eight years, and it is not really as simple as my hon. friend from St. Paul's would perhaps like us to think. There are mechanical difficulties, it is true, as he has pointed out, but for me that has not been the main problem.
The main problem has been how to assure fairness for all taxpayers in the country in connection with this sort of thing. We all have different ideas as to how we should make provision for our later years. Some do it by buying annuities; some work for employers who have pension plans; some buy government bonds, some prefer to invest in equities; and some like to leave their money in the bank.
In principle it might be argued that every Canadian should be entitled, if you will, to have a deduction from his current earnings with respect to savings which he makes in order to provide for his old age. But, as I have pointed out on another occasion, and my hon. friend referred to it today, under certain kinds of savings he is free to use that money for the purchase of a new automobile tomorrow if he changes his mind, or use it to buy a house, or any one of a variety of things.
What the hon. member refers to as mechanical difficulties are mostly the difficulties inherent in working out a plan which would be fair to all Canadian taxpayers. It is not nearly so bad for the man who buys an annuity as is sometimes made out. When the annuity comes due he is taxed only on the interest contained in the annuity. In the case of the approved pension plan he is taxed on the full proceeds. One of the reasons why we made this higher than $900 was, in a sense, to eliminate double taxation.
I can honestly say that nothing would please me more than to be able to find a way of providing this kind of benefit for a self-employed person. I was myself a selfemployed person and a practising lawyer, in the same manner as the hon. member for St. Paul's, and I have had representations from colleagues at the bar, from members of the medical profession and others to the effect that something of this sort ought to be done. But it is not quite so simple, and that is illustrated by the fact that even in the United States they have not been able to find a method of providing a pension deduction for the self-employed.
Income Tax Act

I am sorry to say I have not been able to do better than my colleagues in some other countries, but we have not been able to work out a suitable plan.

This is another relieving section. As my hon. friends know, farmers and fishermen have the privilege of averaging their income over a period of five years, and they can carry losses backward and forward. They can carry it back one year, and forward for a further five years.

Then, let us say, in the fifth year he might have a heavy loss of $8,000 or $10,000, which would more than offset the earnings in the preceding years. He could carry that forward. It is true that farmers, being characteristically cautious people, are not overly optimistic. Perhaps he might fear that he really would not get a chance to offset that in future years, and he has asserted that he should be able to offset the loss in the final year against the profits which he has made in the preceding four years. I would have to get out last year's statute and study it and compare it with this one, but I am taking the assurance which is given me that the effect of the amendment made last year was to narrow the penalty down to the loss of one year. There must be some penalty and there should be some penalty for late filing. It is well-known that the tax returns should be filed, and every other taxpayer pays some penalty for late filing. In a case such as this what would happen? Say that in the first year of a five-year period a man was taxable he filed the return on time and paid his tax; the same in the second; the same in the third year, and in the fourth year he lost a few thousand dollars. He knew from the very first of the year that things were bad, cattle prices were down, and one thing and another, and he knew he lost a lot of money. As a consequence he said to himself: "1 have not made any money; what is the sense of my filing a return? I do not have to pay a tax. There is no penalty." Then he comes along to the fifth year of his averaging period and he finds out that he got some of that money back. He finally files the fifth year's return on time. Is he then penalized on the year in which he lost money or can he at that time file a return for the fourth year on which he lost $8,000 and was not taxable and still take that year into his averaging profit.

If he carried it backward or forward what would happen in the long run?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make one or two brief remarks on this measure. We have this great asset, the Canadian National Railways, and I think it is the clear duty of the house to vote moneys for capital expenditure. However, as we continue to do so I think it is well for us to remind ourselves occasionally of the increasing investment we have year by year. Therefore I propose to put certain figures on the record taken from a statement prepared by the railway in answer to a question by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) and myself. I will read the total of borrowed capital only as shown in the statement and I will do so in five-year periods.
In 1923 there was a total of $1,406 million, in 1928, $1,609 million, and in 1933, $1,922 million. In that year debt was written off in the amount of $373 million and debt trans- ' ferred to equity capital amounted to $270 million, leaving $1,301 million. In 1942 the amount had gone up to $1,328 million. In 1947 it had gone down to $1,272 million, and in 1951 the total was $1,472 million. In 1952 there was transferred to equity capital $736 million leaving in that year $833 million. Last year the amount had risen to $931 million.
The reason I put these figures on the record is, as I said, that I think it is wise for us to remind ourselves not only of the investment we have at the present time but of the previous amounts which have been forgiven the railway from time to time. As hon. members know, the return on that amount is negligible, although that is no fault of the railway. It is really in the interests of the railway that I think it worth while to put

At the resolution stage, the hon. member for Greenwood asked the Minister of Finance one or two questions, and he was assured an answer would be brought down at this time. A general understanding of this legislation is facilitated in this house not only because the bill comes up annually but it does get the lively attention of one of our larger committees each year, the railways and shipping committee. This year I think they held about five sittings, and as a result they have a very substantial Hansard containing the inquiries that were put to the president of the railway and the large staff that accompanies him to the committee to cover the great variety of questions to which answers are given.
The hon. member for Greenwood the other day asked particularly for a comment upon two points. First of all he made this statement, which appears at page 5392 of Hansard for June 2, 1954:
My understanding is that the $72 million referred to is an amount authorized last year but not expended, and that the Intention of the finance department is to have each year a new statement of the amounts actually required for the year.
I think my hon. friend was seeking assurance that we are not departing this year in this annual bill from the practice of previous legislation of this kind, because I found that my hon. friend has probably outlined the basis of this legislation and the practice under it as well as anyone has done when
Canadian National Railways last year he had this to say, which does indeed describe this act of 1954. The hon. member for Greenwood last year said this, as appears at page 4516 of Hansard for April 29, 1953:
My understanding-and I think this is important -is that the policy under the bill is to make a fresh start each year, that is to say, all the unused authorities of past years are washed out and we make a fresh start each year so that there is no overlapping period and no chance of misunderstanding between the national railways and the Department of Finance as to just what are the authority and scope of the Canadian National Railways.
That is true, and I think when the president of the road submitted the capital budget to the railways and shipping committee this year, the summary of financial commitments authorized for 1954 was presented in a form that makes it a little clearer to the members what is involved. For the first time there was clearly set out in columnar form under two headings the 1954 financial authorizations- I am referring to page 1 of the capital budget which is reproduced on page 122 of the minutes of the 1954 sittings of the railways and shipping committee. There was a separation of the projects not heretofore authorized and brought forth for the first time in 1954, and then another column clearly indicating, both in connection with additions and betterments as well as branch line construction and new equipment, items that were projects previously authorized in former financing bills.
Now, the other question that was raised by the hon. member for Greenwood referred to railway policy in the matter of depreciation account. This, of course, is important because hon. members will find opposite section 4 of the bill an item of $19,900,000, which is described as the amount for depreciation accounts for this year's financing, thus reducing the gross capital requirements for the current year from $241,767,198 to a net of $221,867,198 because these moneys set aside in the depreciation account are available for capital expenditures.
As hon. members know, the national road operates certain lines in the United States, and by reason of United States law it is sometimes necessary to have separate accounting practices for the United States operations. To an extent that is true in the matter of the depreciation account. The system of depreciation also differs between equipment and road property. I should like to describe, first of all, the practice with respect to equipment depreciation. Prior to 1940 it was the general practice of the railway to charge operating expenses with the loss of equipment destroyed or worn out in service when the equipment was retired

Canadian National Railways permanently from service. But effective from 1940 the straight line depreciation on rolling stock and floating equipment was adopted. A similar practice on Canadian National lines in the United States has been in effect for some time because of the regulations of the interstate commerce commission.
Under this method a percentage of the capital cost of the equipment is charged to operating expenses annually throughout the service life of equipment, sufficient to retire the investment loss and salvage value of the worn-out units of equipment. The average service life of railway equipment is approximately 28 years. The average annual depreciation rate is approximately 3-32 per cent of the investment value. Under this system the operating expense account for each year bears a proportionate share of the equipment retirement costs irrespective of the date the equipment is retired. This is the unit method of accounting for equipment retirement and conforms to the general practice followed by class 1 roads of the United States.
In the matter of the depreciation of road property there is a difference between United States and Canadian accounts. In the United States the depreciation for national road property there is at rates approved by the interstate commerce commission for individual roads, which became mandatorily effective on January 1, 1943. The items in each primary account are treated as a group and a composite depreciation rate established. Losses on retirement are charged in their entirety to reserves. The average rate of depreciation is approximately 1-5 per cent per annum on the investment value of the various items of road property.
Now, with respect to the Canadian lines, the loss on retirement of Canadian line road property is charged to operating expenses at the time the units of property are retired from service. This is known as retirement accounting.

most other hon. members in the house, as to the desirability of building the hotel in Montreal. In the debate on the budget I expressed my opposition to the construction of this hotel, and I should like to reiterate that opposition tonight. As I recall, president Donald Gordon of the Canadian National Railways said that the building in Montreal was to be a luxury hotel which would accommodate 2,500 people at banquets and 4,000 people at conventions. It may be that in many respects such a building would be desirable. I agree with my colleague from Saskatoon that it would provide employment and might attract tourists. If the hotel were going to be built out of revenue, I would support the expenditure. But when one looks at section 9(2) it becomes clear that in all probability the taxpayers will ultimately have to pay for this luxury hotel. While the parliamentary assistant said the amount is only $5 million this year, eventually it will be $20 million.
I believe it was two years ago when parliament agreed to a reorganization of the capital stock of the Canadian National Railways. At that time we were told that if a billion odd dollars were changed from bonds into noninterest-bearing stock, the profit and loss position of the C.N.R. in future would be a good deal better. Actually since that time it has been better. In 1952 we made a profit of $142,000 and last year a profit of $244,000. Moreover President Gordon told the railways committee that this year probably the C.N.R. would have a substantial deficit.
I cannot believe it is sound business practice for any company to indulge in luxury expenditures at a time when it is operating at a heavy deficit. It seems to me that this is all the more so when hon. members recall that hotel expenditures of the C.N.R. in past years have not been very profitable. One of the best years the system had was in 1952. With an investment of $31,500,000 they were able to show a profit of only $535,000 and that without charging adequate depreciation. So when Mr. Gordon comes before parliament and asks for permission to build another luxury hotel, I am a bit dubious about the wisdom of granting the funds.
Let me repeat that when the C.N.R. comes before parliament and asks for expenditures to build new railways to open up the country, I support them. But I doubt very much whether the building of this luxury hotel is going to help open up the country in any way. I do not think the people in my constituency would be enthusiastic about an expenditure of this kind, nor do I think that the Canadian taxpayer will receive value for his money if the building is proceeded with.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, clause 3 of this bill is the one which has the meat in it. This is the clause that specifies the age at which allowances for disabled persons can be paid. It also has in it as much as we get by way of a definition of total and permanent disability. It also has in it the means test provisions, together with provisions that make it impossible to receive this allowance at the same time as one is receiving any one of certain other items, such as an allowance under the Blind Persons Act, assistance under the Old Age Assistance Act, an allowance under the War Veterans Allowance Act or a pension under the Old Age Security Act. In addition to that, this is the clause that specifies the maximum amount of the allowance as $40. It also specifies that the federal government will pay up to only 50 per cent of the $40 a month. In other words, I have spelled out my statement that this is the clause that has the meat of this legislation in it.
I wonder whether the minister is in a position now to comment on some of the points that were raised when we were at the second reading stage. Perhaps he could start with one that was raised by members in all parties on this side of the house, namely the question of the definition. The clause reads that the allowance can be paid to a recipient who is "totally and permanently disabled as prescribed by the regulations". In this clause there are other matters that I wish to say something about, namely, the amount of the allowance, the age at which it is payable and the division between the provinces and the federal government. Perhaps the minister might first comment on the remarks made by the hon. member for Lanark, the hon. member for Red Deer, myself and others on the way in which total and permanent disability is defined. I ask him, if he will, to relate his comments to the remarks made on this 83276-355J
Disabled Persons-Allowances question in the brief presented to the government by the Canadian Welfare Council to which I made reference last Tuesday.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
On clause 3 I have a question which I should like to raise for the minister's consideration. Subsection 2 provides that payment shall be made only in respect of a recipient who-and I then drop down to paragraph (f) which reads as follows:
(f) is not a patient or resident in a hospital, nursing home, or private, charitable or public institution, except as prescribed in the regulations.
I do not know what stage the drafting of regulations has reached, but many instances readily come to my mind where a disabled person who receives a pension would be much better off and would be better cared for in a private charitable institution than elsewhere. I have some instances of that kind in mind from my own experience. I know that some of these institutions which keep elderly people who have the old age pension look after them very well on part of the pension and leave the pensioners with a certain part of it as spending money. It is a happy arrangement for elderly people and I think it would apply equally well to disabled people who would be looked after well in these private institutions by reason of the pension which they get under this act; whereas if the pension is not permitted to be paid when they are in such homes, it seems to me that one of the purposes of the act is defeated.
I appreciate the fact that one does not wish to duplicate the expenditure of public funds for disabled persons by having them maintained at public expense in a home and also by paying a pension. But if only a modest part of the funds of a home are public funds, it seems to me that it is a proper case for paying the pension. I trust that the minister has that point in mind and will deal with it in the regulations.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext: Further to the remarks made by the hon. member, may I say that this morning I had a letter which set out the case of a disabled war veteran-one who is 100 per cent disabled-who is contributing to the keep of a totally disabled wife in an institution. Something should be done under this act to deal with a matter of that kind. It does not seem fair that he should be contributing for that purpose part of his pension

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Disabled Persons-Allowances paid to him for war wounds and for other disability. He has what amounts to 100 per cent disability.
When the bill was before the house we mentioned this question of the time between the age of 16 when the family allowance stops and when this bill entitles the recipient to receive the pension at 18. I maintain that those two years are important years in the training and care of the disabled person and that those two years could be lost to some degree in the training of a disabled person or with respect to his health. Those two years are just as important as are any other years and during them they are not receiving anything.
The other point is this. If some information were given by the minister as to just what is meant by totally and permanently disabled people, it possibly would help us in this discussion. There is one other matter I wish to mention. I did not get a chance to say anything about it at the time, but there has been some discussion about who is responsible for this bill. I should like to pay tribute to one person who has worked consistently through the years. That person is Miss Eva Warden of Calgary who brought this delegation down to the house. I do not like to use the word "lobby" but she worked very hard in this matter. I believe in giving honour where honour is due; and I believe that Miss Warden should receive great credit for what she has done in promoting public opinion with respect to the bringing in of this bill.

Mr. Chairman, last week I expressed the hope that the minister would be able to give us some information at least to indicate the extent of the agreement that has been reached between his department and the provinces in connection with this matter of the defining of the expression "totally and permanently disabled as prescribed by the regulations". Personally I am confident, without having been told, that some measure of agreement was reached. Undoubtedly this matter came up for serious consideration. In the second place, I should like to know whether, in the course of discussing the matter, it was agreed tentatively at least to go as far as the Alberta act does in its present statute, that is, as amended at the last session. That brings me to the specific subject of the case where a person may be partially disabled physically and partially disabled mentally, but not sufficiently mentally ill to warrant being placed in an institution. Nevertheless that person is permanently disabled. I should like to

know whether or not that type of case will be included in the definition.
Clause stands.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we shall continue in the morning with this debate followed by the legislation with respect to benefits for the armed forces, then the National Harbours Board Act, and then the Post Office Act. As the house knows, there is a pension bill in the veterans affairs committee that is being reported with a suggested amendment which, if His Excellency concurs, would be recommended to the house tomorrow by consent, I hope, and might be dealt with at the resolution stage so that the pension bill can be dealt with in committee of the whole with the amendment.
Then we have a bill, of which notice has been given, with respect to motor vehicle transportation. It would be our hope that hon. members opposite might find it convenient to deal with that some time later in the day after they have had an opportunity to see it. If these matters are all disposed of we shall take estimates, beginning with national revenue, then secretary of state, fisheries, and mines and technical surveys.

Mr. Speaker, the motor transport bill has not yet been distributed. The minister was kind enough to give me a copy but I understand it has not been distributed generally. Therefore it would be very difficult to go on with that tomorrow. It was my understanding also that the Post Office Act would be taken before the national harbours board bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I know that some hon. members have committee work to attend to in the morning, and if it is not found possible to have them here at the time they have particular matters to discuss we can arrange that. However, we might leave the order I have indicated for the time being. We shall see that copies of the bill with respect to motor vehicle transportation are available the first thing in the morning, if they are not now available when hon. members leave the chamber. I am sure that the intelligent consideration which you will give to it in the meantime will lead you to be able to discuss it in the afternoon.
